{{short description|Operation in complex geometry}}

In [[complex geometry]], the '''complex conjugate line''' of a [[straight line]] is the line that it becomes by taking the [[complex conjugate]] of each point on this line.<ref>{{citation|title=Linear Algebra and Geometry|first1=Igor R.|last1=Shafarevich|first2=Alexey|last2=Remizov|first3=David P.|last3=Kramer|first4=Lena|last4=Nekludova|publisher=Springer|year=2012|isbn=9783642309946|page=413|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6Pp2-DTOKWIC&pg=PA413}}.</ref>

This is the same as taking the complex conjugates of the [[coefficients]] of the line. So if the equation of {{math|D}} is {{math|1=D: ''ax'' + ''by'' + ''cz'' = 0}}, then the equation of its conjugate {{math|D*}} is {{math|1=D*: ''a*x'' + ''b*y'' + ''c*z'' = 0}}.

The conjugate of a [[real line]] is the line itself.
The [[Line–line intersection|intersection point]] of two conjugated lines is always real.<ref>{{citation|title=A Mathematician Grappling With His Century|first=Laurent|last=Schwartz|publisher=Springer|year=2001|isbn=9783764360528|page=52|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xVrC7ek7iRwC&pg=PA52}}.</ref>
